It may happen that the class \( \mathcal{G}_G(\Omega) \) is empty. This happens when \( 0 \notin \operatorname{int} \Omega \). This is because if \( f \) is positive definite, then \( |f(g)| \leq f(0) \) for all \( g \in G \), and if \( 0 \notin \operatorname{int} \Omega \), then \( f(0) = 0 \), and hence \( f \) is identically 0. In which case, the class \( \mathcal{G}_G(\Omega) \) is empty because \( f(0) = 1 \) can not hold for a continuous positive definite function \( f \) with \( f_+ \) supported in \( \Omega \). On the other hand, if \( \Omega \) is a neighbourhood of 0, i.e., \( 0 \in \operatorname{int} \Omega \), then there is a symmetric neighbourhood \( U \) of 0 such that \( U + U \subset \Omega \). Then the convolution \( 1_U * 1_U \) of the characteristic function \( 1_U \) of \( U \) with itself is a continuous positive definite function supported in \( \Omega \). We can normalise it to obtain a function that

belongs to \( G_G(\Omega) \). In other words, the class \( G_G(\Omega) \) is nonempty if and only if \( \Omega \) is a neighbourhood of 0.
results.route_rationale: Crisp formalisable core: positive definiteness implies $|f(g)|\le f(0)$, which drives the emptiness criterion.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised the paper's inequality $|f(g)|\le f(0)$ directly from the paper's own definition of positive definiteness (the finite double-sum condition, transcribed verbatim, with $\ge 0$ for a complex quantity rendered via Mathlib's `ComplexOrder`, i.e. real part nonnegative and imaginary part zero). No extra hypotheses were added: $G$ is an arbitrary `AddCommGroup`, no continuity or topology assumed. The Lean proof reconstructs the classical argument: $n=1$ gives $0\le f(0)$; $n=2$ at the points $0,x$ with $c=(1,1)$ and $c=(1,i)$ forces Hermitian symmetry $f(-x)=\overline{f(x)}$; then $c=(1,t\overline{f(x)})$ for real $t$ gives $0\le(1+t^2\|f(x)\|^2)\,\mathrm{Re}\,f(0)+2t\|f(x)\|^2$, and $t=-1/\|f(x)\|$ yields $\|f(x)\|\le \mathrm{Re}\,f(0)$. The corollary `eq_zero_of_f_zero_eq_zero` formalises the paper's very next inference, that $f(0)=0$ forces $f\equiv 0$. Compiled clean: no errors, no `sorry`, axioms exactly [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. The paper's reasoning is formally confirmed.

holds for all continuous compactly supported functions \( h \) on \( G \). According to [17, Theorem 1.7.3] an integrally positive definite function agrees locally almost everywhere with a continuous positive definite function. When \( G \) is \( \sigma \)-compact, locally almost everywhere is the same as almost everywhere. Therefore, on a \( \sigma \)-compact group an integrally positive definite function agrees almost everywhere with a continuous positive definite function. The approach to the main problem of this paper is to reduce the problem to the case of \( \sigma \)-compact LCA groups and then extend the solution to the general case. Recall that a LCA group \( G \) is \( \sigma \)-compact if it can be written as a countable union of compact sets.

The strengthening from 'locally almost everywhere' to 'almost everywhere' under $\sigma$-compactness is correct: a $\sigma$-compact group is a countable union of compacta, and a set that is locally null is null on each compactum, hence null. This is precisely why the paper reduces to the $\sigma$-compact case first (Theorem 3) before applying Theorem 8. Internally consistent; no error.

LEMMA 1 (see [10, Lemma 6 and proof of Theorem 2]). Let \( H \) be an open subgroup of a LCA group \( G \), and let \( \Omega \) be a subset of \( H \). If a function \( \varphi : H \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) is in \( \mathcal{G}_H(\Omega) \), then its trivial extension \( \tilde{\varphi} : G \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) is in \( \mathcal{G}_G(\Omega) \).

PROOF. Suppose that \( \varphi : H \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) is in \( \mathcal{G}_H(\Omega) \). In particular, \( \varphi \) is continuous, positive definite, has \( \operatorname{supp} \varphi_+ \subset \Omega \), and satisfies \( \varphi(0) = 1 \). Clearly, its trivial extension has \( \operatorname{supp} \tilde{\varphi}_+ \subset \Omega \), and satisfies \( \tilde{\varphi}(0) = 1 \). To see that \( \tilde{\varphi} \) is continuous, note that \( H \), being an open subgroup, is also closed, and hence its complement \( G \setminus H \) is open. Now, \( \tilde{\varphi} \) is continuous at all \( g \in H \) because it coincides with the continuous function \( \varphi : H \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) on the open set \( H \). It is continuous at all \( g \in G \setminus H \) because it is identically 0 on the open set \( G \setminus H \). It is positive definite by [13, Theorem 32.43(a)]. □
results.route_rationale: Trivial extension lemma; the positive-definiteness step is an external citation, the rest is point-set topology.

fallback_result.reasoning: Lemma 1 and its proof. Each clause checks out: (i) $\operatorname{supp}\tilde\varphi_+ = \operatorname{supp}\varphi_+\subset\Omega$ since $\tilde\varphi=0$ off $H$; (ii) $\tilde\varphi(0)=\varphi(0)=1$ as $0\in H$; (iii) continuity -- an open subgroup is also closed (its complement is a union of open cosets), so $G\setminus H$ is open and $\tilde\varphi$ is locally equal to a continuous function on each of the two open sets $H$ and $G\setminus H$, which cover $G$; (iv) positive definiteness by [13, Theorem 32.43(a)]. Integrability, needed for $\tilde\varphi\in\mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)$, follows from $\int_G|\tilde\varphi|\,d\lambda_G=\int_H|\varphi|\,d\lambda_H<\infty$; the paper omits mentioning it but it is immediate. No error.

LEMMA 2. Let \( G \) be a LCA group, and let \( (K_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) be a sequence of \( \sigma \)-compact subsets of \( G \). The group \( H \) generated by the union \( \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} K_n \) is \( \sigma \)-compact. Furthermore, if at least one of the \( K_n \)'s has non-empty interior, then \( H \) is open.

Lemma 2 is standard and the interested reader may consult the proof of [7, Proposition 1.2.1(c)].
results.route_rationale: Standard topological-group fact, explicitly delegated to [7, Proposition 1.2.1(c)].

fallback_result.reasoning: Lemma 2: the subgroup $H$ generated by $\bigcup_n K_n$ of $\sigma$-compact sets is $\sigma$-compact, and open if some $K_n$ has nonempty interior. Both halves are correct. $\sigma$-compactness: $H=\bigcup_{m}(S\cup -S)^m$ where $S=\bigcup_n K_n$ is $\sigma$-compact, and finite sums of $\sigma$-compact sets are $\sigma$-compact (a finite product of compacta is compact and the sum map is continuous), so $H$ is a countable union of compacta. Openness: if some $K_n$ has nonempty interior then $H$ contains a nonempty open set, and a subgroup with nonempty interior is open (translate the interior around by group elements). No error.

THEOREM 3. Let G be a LCA group, and Ω a subset of G of finite Haar measure. There is an open σ-compact subgroup H of G containing Ω such that

(1)  \( D_G(\Omega) = D_H(\Omega) \).
results.route_rationale: Reduction-to-$\sigma$-compact statement; the formal content is the construction in its proof.

fallback_result.reasoning: Theorem 3: for $\Omega\subset G$ of finite Haar measure there is an open $\sigma$-compact subgroup $H\supset\Omega$ with $\mathcal{D}_G(\Omega)=\mathcal{D}_H(\Omega)$. The statement is coherent and correctly does NOT require $\Omega$ closed (closedness is only needed from Theorem 8 onward, as the paper itself flags). Note $H$ open implies $\lambda_H:=\lambda_G|_H$ is a Haar measure on $H$, and interiors relative to $H$ agree with interiors relative to $G$ for subsets of $H$ -- both facts are used in the proof and both hold. No error.

results.content:
PROOF. By outer regularity of the Haar measure on G, there is an open identity neighbourhood U in G containing Ω with \( \lambda_G(U) < \infty \). We claim that U lies in an open σ-compact subgroup. To see this, let K be some σ-compact open subgroup of G. One may always obtain such a K by considering a relatively compact symmetric identity neighbourhood V and observing that the union

\( K := \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} nV \)

is an open σ-compact subgroup. Now, note that G is a disjoint union of cosets g + K of K with g running through a set of coset representatives of K. Since the cosets of K are disjoint and cover G, the collection of subsets (g + K) ∩ U of U as g runs through the set of coset representatives of K are disjoint and their union is U. Now, either (g + K) ∩ U = ∅ or \( \lambda_G((g + K) \cap U) > 0 \) because (g + K) ∩ U is open, and every open set is either empty or has strictly positive measure. Hence (g + K) ∩ U ≠ ∅ for at most countably many cosets g + K of K, otherwise this would contradict the finiteness of the Haar measure of U. Clearly, U is contained in the subgroup generated by the union of K and the at most countably many open σ-compact cosets g + K of K that meet U nontrivially. Denote this subgroup by H and observe that it is open and σ-compact by Lemma 2. Equip H with Haar measure \( \lambda_H := \lambda_G|_H \). By construction, Ω ⊂ H.

Let us first consider the case when 0 ∉ int Ω. Then, both \( \mathcal{G}_G(\Omega) \) and \( \mathcal{G}_H(\Omega) \) are empty. Therefore, both sides of (1) are equal to 0, and the theorem is proved in this case. Now assume that 0 ∈ int Ω, so that both \( \mathcal{G}_G(\Omega) \) and \( \mathcal{G}_H(\Omega) \) are nonempty.
results.route_rationale: Construction of $H$ via Haar outer regularity and a coset-counting argument; LCA/Haar machinery outside Mathlib's reach.

fallback_result.reasoning: Construction of $H$. Checked step by step. (a) $K:=\bigcup_{n\ge1}nV$ for a relatively compact symmetric open identity neighbourhood $V$ is an open subgroup ($nV+mV\subset(n+m)V$, $-nV=nV$, $0\in V$) and is $\sigma$-compact, since $\overline V\subset V+V$ gives $n\overline V\subset 2nV\subset K$, so $K=\bigcup_n n\overline V$ is a countable union of compacta. (b) The sets $(g+K)\cap U$ over coset representatives are disjoint with union $U$, each open, hence empty or of strictly positive Haar measure. (c) The countability step is correct although stated briefly: if uncountably many disjoint sets $A_i\subset U$ had $\lambda_G(A_i)>0$, then $I_n=\{i:\lambda_G(A_i)>1/n\}$ has at most $n\lambda_G(U)$ elements, so $I=\bigcup_n I_n$ would be countable -- contradiction. (d) Lemma 2 then makes $H$ open and $\sigma$-compact. Two cosmetic gaps, neither erratum-level: outer regularity yields an open $U\supset\Omega$ of finite measure but not automatically an identity neighbourhood (replace $U$ by $U\cup V$), and the degenerate case uses the convention $\sup\emptyset=0$. No mathematical error.

First, let \( (f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) be a \( D_G(\Omega) \)-extremal sequence in \( \mathcal{G}_G(\Omega) \) such that

\[
\int_G f_n(g) d\lambda_G(g) \geq D_G(\Omega) - \frac{1}{n} \quad \text{for all } n \in \mathbb{N}.
\]

Let \( f_n|_H : H \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) denote the restriction of \( f_n \) to H. Observe that for all n ∈ ℕ, we have

(2)  \(
\int_G f_n(g) d\lambda_G(g) = \int_H f_n(g) d\lambda_G(g) + \int_{G \setminus H} f_n(g) d\lambda_G(g),
\)

Analysis Mathematica 51, 2025

and since supp(f_n)_+ is contained in H, we have that f_n(g) ≤ 0 for all g ∈ G\H. Therefore, 

(3)  ∫_{G\H} f_n(g) dλ_G(g) ≤ 0.

From (2) and (3) it follows that

(4)  ∫_H f_n|_H(g) dλ_H(g) = ∫_H f_n(g) dλ_G(g) ≥ ∫_G f_n(g) dλ_G(g).

Now, by the definition of D_H(Ω) and inequality (4), we have

D_H(Ω) ≥ ∫_H f_n|_H(g) dλ_H(g) ≥ ∫_G f_n(g) dλ_G(g) ≥ D_G(Ω) - 1/n.

Thus D_H(Ω) ≥ D_G(Ω).
results.route_rationale: Abstract measure-theoretic content, cleanly formalisable: split the integral over $H$ and $G\setminus H$ and use nonpositivity off $H$.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised equations (2), (3) and (4) as one statement in abstract measure theory, which is exactly the generality the paper's argument uses: $H$ measurable (the paper's $H$ is an open subgroup, hence measurable), $f$ integrable, and $f\le 0$ on $H^c=G\setminus H$ -- the latter being the paper's own justification 'since $\operatorname{supp}(f_n)_+$ is contained in $H$, we have that $f_n(g)\le 0$ for all $g\in G\setminus H$'. Eq. (2) is `integral_add_compl`; eq. (3) follows from `integral_nonpos_of_ae` after restricting the a.e. bound to $H^c$; eq. (4) is then linear arithmetic. The identification $\int_H f|_H\,d\lambda_H=\int_H f\,d\lambda_G$ in (4) is definitional once $\lambda_H=\lambda_G|_H$, as the paper sets up. Compiled clean, no `sorry`, standard axioms only. All three assertions confirmed, including the direction of the inequality in (4).

LEMMA 4 [17, Theorem 1.4.3]. Let G be a LCA group and f a continuous positive definite function on G. Let V be a symmetric neighborhood of 0 with compact closure and set χ := 1_V/λ_G(V) where 1_V is the characteristic function of V. Then the inequality

|f(x) - f * χ(x)|^2 ≤ 2f(0)λ_G(V)^{-1} ∫_V (f(0) - Re f(g)) dλ_G(g)

holds for all x ∈ G.
results.route_rationale: Quoted from [17, Theorem 1.4.3]; the checkable content is whether the inequality as transcribed is right.

fallback_result.reasoning: Lemma 4: $|f(x)-f*\chi(x)|^2 \le 2f(0)\lambda_G(V)^{-1}\int_V(f(0)-\operatorname{Re} f(g))\,d\lambda_G(g)$ with $\chi=1_V/\lambda_G(V)$, $V$ symmetric with compact closure. I checked the transcription (in particular the constant $2$, the most likely place for a transcription slip) in three ways. (i) Since $V$ is symmetric, $\lambda_G(V)^{-1}\int_V(f(0)-\operatorname{Re} f) = f(0)-\operatorname{Re}(f*\chi)(0)$, so the right-hand side is $2f(0)[f(0)-\operatorname{Re}(f*\chi)(0)]$, the familiar form of Rudin's estimate. (ii) At $x=0$ the inequality reads $u^2\le 2f(0)u$ with $u=f(0)-\operatorname{Re}(f*\chi)(0)\ge 0$, which holds exactly because $|f*\chi(0)|\le f(0)$ -- so the constant $2$ is sharp enough to be the right one and not a weakened or strengthened variant. (iii) Numerically on $G=\mathbb{R}$, $V=(-a,a)$: for $f=\cos$ the inequality becomes $(1-\tfrac{\sin a}{a})^2\le 2(1-\tfrac{\sin a}{a})$, and for $f=e^{-|x|}$ it becomes $u^2\le 2u$ with $u=1-\tfrac{1-e^{-a}}{a}$; both hold for all $a>0$. Correctly transcribed; no error.

LEMMA 5 (compare [17, Lemma 1.5.1]). Let \( G \) be a LCA group. Let \( k \in L^2(G) \), and let \( (\varphi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) be a sequence in \( L^2(G) \) with \( \|\varphi_n\|_{L^2(G)} \leq C \) for all \( n \in \mathbb{N} \). If the sequence \( (\varphi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) converges weakly in \( L^2(G) \) to a function \( \varphi \in L^2(G) \), then the sequence \( (k * \varphi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) converges to \( k * \varphi \) uniformly on the compact subsets of \( G \).

PROOF. For \( h \in L^2(G) \), define
\[
L(h) := \int_G h(g)\varphi(-g) \, d\lambda_G(g), \quad L_n(h) := \int_G h(g)\varphi_n(-g) \, d\lambda_G(g).
\]
The functionals \( L \) and \( L_n \) are continuous with respect to the norm topology on \( L^2(G) \). By Hölder's inequality, \( |L_n(h)| \leq C\|h\|_{L^2(G)} \) for all \( n \in \mathbb{N} \). Therefore, by the Uniform Boundedness Principle, the family \( \{L_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \) is equicontinuous on \( L^2(G) \). Note that weak convergence of \( (\varphi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) to \( \varphi \) is equivalent to pointwise convergence of \( L_n \) to \( L \), and that pointwise convergence together with equicontinuity of \( (L_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) implies that \( (L_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) converges to \( L \) uniformly on the compact subsets of \( L^2(G) \). Let \( K \) be a compact subset of \( G \). The mapping \( G \ni x \mapsto {}_x k \in L^2(G) \), where \( {}_x k \) denotes the left translate of \( k \) by an element \( x \in G \) and given by \( {}_x k(g) = k(x + g) \) for all \( g \in G \), is continuous and hence the set \( \{{}_x k : x \in K\} \) is compact in the norm topology of \( L^2(G) \). The uniform convergence on \( K \) of \( (k * \varphi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) now follows from the equations
\[
k * \varphi_n(x) = \int_G k(x + g)\varphi_n(-g) \, d\lambda_G(g) = L_n({}_x k)
\]
and
\[
k * \varphi(x) = L({}_x k). \quad \Box
\]
results.route_rationale: Weak-$L^2$ convergence transferred through convolution; functional analysis on an LCA group, not formalisable in Mathlib as stated.

fallback_result.reasoning: Lemma 5 and its proof. The computation that carries the argument, $k*\varphi_n(x)=\int_G k(x+g)\varphi_n(-g)\,d\lambda_G(g)=L_n({}_xk)$, is correct: substituting $y=x+g$ in $k*\varphi_n(x)=\int k(y)\varphi_n(x-y)\,d\lambda_G(y)$ gives exactly that, and it matches the definition $L_n(h)=\int h(g)\varphi_n(-g)\,d\lambda_G(g)$ with $h={}_xk$. The equivalence of weak $L^2$ convergence with pointwise convergence of $L_n$ is correct because $h\mapsto\overline{h(-\cdot)}$ is a bijection of $L^2(G)$. Continuity of $x\mapsto{}_xk$ in $L^2$ makes $\{{}_xk:x\in K\}$ compact, and pointwise convergence plus equicontinuity gives uniform convergence on compacta. One redundancy: the Uniform Boundedness Principle is invoked to get equicontinuity that the preceding Holder bound $|L_n(h)|\le C\|h\|_{L^2}$ already supplies. That is stylistic, not an error. No error.

THEOREM 6 (compare [17, Theorem 1.5.2]). Let \( G \) be a LCA group. If a sequence \( (f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \) of continuous positive definite functions on \( G \) converges weakly in \( L^2(G) \) to a continuous positive definite function \( f \) and \( \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(0) = f(0) \), then this sequence converges to \( f \) uniformly on the compact subsets of \( G \).

PROOF. Let \( K \) be a fixed compact subset of \( G \). For any function \( h \) on \( G \), write \( \|h\|_K := \sup\{|h(g)| : g \in K\} \) and \( \|h\|_\infty := \sup\{|h(g)| : g \in G\} \). We show that
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \|f_n - f\|_K = 0.
\]

Let V and χ be as in Lemma 4. We have
\[
\|f_n - f\|_K \leq \|f_n - f_n * \chi\|_\infty + \|f_n * \chi - f * \chi\|_K + \|f * \chi - f\|_\infty.
\]

Now let ε > 0 be arbitrary. By the continuity of f, we can choose V small enough so that

\[
2f(0)\lambda_G(V)^{-1} \int_V (f(0) - \operatorname{Re} f(g))\,d\lambda_G(g) < \frac{\varepsilon^2}{9}.
\]

From Lemma 4, we have

\[
\|f * \chi - f\|_\infty < \frac{\varepsilon}{3}.
\]

Since (f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} converges to f weakly in L^2(G) and \(\lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(0) = f(0)\), there exists an N > 0 such that for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(n > N\) we have

\[
2f_n(0)\lambda_G(V)^{-1} \int_V (f_n(0) - \operatorname{Re} f_n(g))\,d\lambda_G(g) < \frac{\varepsilon^2}{9}.
\]

Applying Lemma 4 again, we get

\[
\|f_n - f_n * \chi\|_\infty < \frac{\varepsilon}{3}.
\]

By Lemma 5, there exists M > N such that for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(n > M\) we have

\[
\|f_n * \chi - f * \chi\|_K < \frac{\varepsilon}{3}.
\]

Altogether, we conclude that \(\|f_n - f\|_K < \varepsilon\) for all \(n > M\), showing that \((f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) converges uniformly on the compact subset K. □
results.route_rationale: The $\varepsilon/3$ argument; crisp but built on Lemma 4/5 and LCA-group convolution.

fallback_result.reasoning: Theorem 6 and proof. The triangle split $\|f_n-f\|_K\le\|f_n-f_n*\chi\|_\infty+\|f_n*\chi-f*\chi\|_K+\|f*\chi-f\|_\infty$ is valid, and each term is bounded by $\varepsilon/3$. The numerology is consistent: the hypothesis bounds are $<\varepsilon^2/9$ and Lemma 4 bounds a *square*, so $\sqrt{\varepsilon^2/9}=\varepsilon/3$ is the correct extraction, and because the bound is uniform in $x$ the strict inequality survives passing to the supremum. The step asserting the $f_n$ analogue of the smallness condition for large $n$ is legitimate: $1_V\in L^2(G)$ as $V$ is relatively compact, so weak $L^2$ convergence gives $\int_V\operatorname{Re}f_n\to\int_V\operatorname{Re}f$, and together with $f_n(0)\to f(0)$ the whole expression converges to the quantity already known to be $<\varepsilon^2/9$. The $L^2$-boundedness Lemma 5 requires is automatic since weakly convergent sequences are bounded. Order of quantifiers ($V$ chosen from $\varepsilon$ and $f$ first, then $N$, then $M>N$) is correct. No error.

## LEMMA 7 (Mazur's lemma, see [5, Corollary 3.8 and Exercise 3.4]).
Let E be a Banach space and let \((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence in E converging to \(x \in E\) weakly. Then there exists a sequence \((y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) in E such that

\[
y_n \in \operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=n}^{\infty} \{x_i\}\right)\quad \text{for all } n \in \mathbb{N},
\]
and \((y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) converges strongly to x.
results.route_rationale: Quoted from [5]; no Mathlib counterpart, and nothing to check beyond faithfulness of the statement.

fallback_result.reasoning: Lemma 7 (Mazur): for $x_n\to x$ weakly in a Banach space there are $y_n\in\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i\ge n}\{x_i\})$ with $y_n\to x$ strongly. This is the standard form of the lemma and is correctly stated, including the essential detail that the convex hull is taken over the *tail* $i\ge n$ -- which is what lets the paper conclude that the new sequence inherits extremality. The use made of it is legitimate: $\mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)$ is convex (if $f,g\le 0$ off $\Omega$ then so is any convex combination, and $P_1$ is convex), so the $y_n$ stay in the class. No error.

## THEOREM 8.
Let G be a σ-compact LCA group and Ω a closed neighbourhood of 0 with finite Haar measure. Then there exists an extremal function for \(D_G(\Omega)\). Moreover, the extremal function can be approximated uniformly on the compact subsets of G by a \(D_G(\Omega)\)-extremal sequence.
results.route_rationale: Main $\sigma$-compact existence statement; the verifiable content is distributed over its proof steps.

fallback_result.reasoning: Theorem 8: for $G$ $\sigma$-compact and $\Omega$ a closed neighbourhood of $0$ with finite Haar measure, an extremal function for $\mathcal{D}_G(\Omega)$ exists and is approximable uniformly on compacta by an extremal sequence. The hypotheses are exactly the ones the proof consumes: $\sigma$-compactness for the integrally-positive-definite regularisation, closedness of $\Omega$ for $\operatorname{supp} f_+\subset\Omega$, neighbourhood-of-$0$ for nonemptiness and for $\mathcal{D}_G(\Omega)>0$, finite measure for the $L^2$ bound and dominated convergence. Statement is sound. No error.

results.content:
Since $\mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)$ is contained in a closed, bounded, and hence a weakly sequentially compact subset of $L^2(G)$, the sequence $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ has a subsequence converging weakly in $L^2(G)$ to some $f \in L^2(G)$. By replacing $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ by this subsequence, we assume that $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges weakly in $L^2(G)$ to $f$. Since $\mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)$ is a convex subset of $L^2(G)$, Lemma 7 implies that there is a sequence $(h_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)$ chosen such that $h_n \in \mathrm{conv}(\bigcup_{i=n}^{\infty} f_i)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and converging to $f$ strongly in $L^2(G)$. We claim that the latter sequence is $D_G(\Omega)$-extremal. First note that by the extremality of $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, we have that for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n > N$ it holds that

\[
\left| \int_G f_n(g) d\lambda_G(g) - D_G(\Omega) \right| < \varepsilon.
\]

Now, write $h_n = \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} c_k^n f_k$, where $c_k^n \geq 0$, $\sum_{k=n}^{\infty} c_k^n = 1$, and $c_k^n = 0$ for all but finitely many $k \geq n$. Then for any $n > N$, we have

\[
\left| \int_G h_n(g) d\lambda_G(g) - D_G(\Omega) \right| \leq \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} c_k^n \left| \int_G f_k(g) d\lambda_G(g) - D_G(\Omega) \right| < \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} c_k^n \varepsilon = \varepsilon.
\]

Therefore $(h_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is $D_G(\Omega)$-extremal. So, replacing, if necessary, the sequence $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ by this new sequence $(h_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, assume that $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $f$ strongly in $L^2(G)$. By passing to a pointwise almost everywhere convergent subsequence, assume that $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $f$ pointwise almost everywhere. The fact that $|f_n(g)| \leq 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $g \in G$, and that $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges almost everywhere to $f$ implies that $f$ is bounded in $L^{\infty}(G)$ by 1.
results.route_rationale: Fully formalisable finite-convex-combination estimate; the inequality chain is where a slip would show.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised the paper's displayed estimate $|\int h_n-D|\le\sum_k c_k^n|\int f_k-D|<\sum_k c_k^n\varepsilon=\varepsilon$, writing $a\,k$ for $\int_G f_k\,d\lambda_G$ and $D$ for $\mathcal{D}_G(\Omega)$. The paper's finite-support condition ('$c_k^n=0$ for all but finitely many $k\ge n$') is rendered as a `Finset` index set, which is faithful. Both claimed inequalities were proved, including the strictness of the second: the key point is that $\sum_{k\in s}c_k=1>0$ forces some $c_{k_0}>0$, which is what licenses `Finset.sum_lt_sum` and hence the strict inequality -- the paper writes '<' and this is justified. Compiled clean, no `sorry`, standard axioms only. The estimate, and therefore the conclusion that $(h_n)$ is again $\mathcal{D}_G(\Omega)$-extremal, is confirmed.

Since $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges weakly in $L^2(G)$ to $f$, it follows that $f$ is integrally positive definite. The function $f$ being integrally positive definite and $G$ being $\sigma$-compact implies that $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a continuous positive definite function. Thus, by correcting $f$ on a set of Haar measure zero, thus not changing the value of its integral, assume that $f$ is a continuous positive definite function. Continuity of $f$ and the fact that $f$ is a pointwise almost everywhere limit of the functions $f_n$, each of which satisfying $\operatorname{supp}(f_n)_+ \subset \Omega$, implies that $\operatorname{supp} f_+ \subset \Omega$. Since $\operatorname{supp} f_+ \subset \Omega$ we have

\[
(5) \quad \int_G f_+(g) d\lambda_G(g) = \int_{\Omega} f_+(g) d\lambda_G(g) \leq \lambda_G(\Omega) < \infty.
\]

On the other hand, by Fatou's lemma

(6)  \[\int_G f_-(g)\,d\lambda_G(g) \leq \liminf_{n\to\infty} \int_G (f_n)_-(g)\,d\lambda_G(g)\]
    \[\leq \liminf_{n\to\infty} \int_G (f_n)_+(g)\,d\lambda_G(g) \leq \lambda_G(\Omega) < \infty,\]

where the second inequality of (6) is obtained using that \(f_n\) being positive definite and integrable implies that

\[
0 \leq \int_G f_n(g)\, d\lambda_G(g) = \int_G (f_n)_+(g)\, d\lambda_G(g) - \int_G (f_n)_-(g)\, d\lambda_G(g).
\]

Together, (5) and (6) imply that

\[
\int_G |f(g)|\, d\lambda_G(g) = \int_G f_+(g)\, d\lambda_G(g) + \int_G f_-(g)\, d\lambda_G(g) < \infty.
\]
results.route_rationale: Fatou chain plus the positive/negative-part bookkeeping; all four links are formalisable.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised every link of the paper's chain. (5): $\int f_+\le\lambda_G(\Omega)$ from $f\le 1$ and $\{f>0\}\subseteq\Omega$ -- proved by dominating $f_+$ pointwise by $1_\Omega$, the case $x\notin\Omega$ using that the support hypothesis forces $f(x)\le 0$. (6) first inequality: Fatou's lemma, discharged by Mathlib's `lintegral_liminf_le`, which is the inequality the paper cites and in the direction the paper uses it. (6) second inequality: the paper's justification $0\le\int f_n=\int(f_n)_+-\int(f_n)_-$ indeed gives $\int(f_n)_-\le\int(f_n)_+$. (6) last inequality: a sequence bounded above by $M$ has $\liminf\le M$. Finally $\int|f|=\int f_++\int f_-$ via the pointwise identity $|t|=\max(t,0)+\max(-t,0)$, so both bounds being finite gives $f\in L^1$. All six declarations compiled clean with no `sorry` and standard axioms only. The chain is confirmed; in particular the second inequality of (6), the one the paper pauses to justify, is correct.

Therefore, \(f \in L^1(G)\). Next, we show that \(f \in \mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)\) and that it is extremal. To that end, note that the sequence \(\big((f_n)_+\big)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) of the positive parts of the \(f_n\)'s converges pointwise almost everywhere to \(f_+\), and that \((f_n)_+ \leq 1_\Omega\). Therefore, by Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem and \(\lambda_G(\Omega) < \infty\), we have

(7)  \[\int_G f_+(g)\,d\lambda_G(g) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_G (f_n)_+(g)\,d\lambda_G(g).\]

Recall that from (6) we have the inequality

(8)  \[\int_G f_-(g)\,d\lambda_G(g) \leq \liminf_{n\to\infty} \int_G (f_n)_-(g)\,d\lambda_G(g).\]

Now, subtracting (8) from (7) we have

\[
\int_G f(g)\,d\lambda_G(g) \geq \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_G (f_n)_+(g)\,d\lambda_G(g)
- \liminf_{n\to\infty} \int_G (f_n)_-(g)\,d\lambda_G(g)
\]

\[
= \limsup_{n\to\infty} \int_G \big((f_n)_+(g) - (f_n)_-(g)\big)\,d\lambda_G(g)
\]

\[
= \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_G f_n(g)\,d\lambda_G(g) = D_G(\Omega).
\]

Hypotheses are the ones the paper has already established: $a\to A$ is its eq. (7) (dominated convergence against $1_\Omega$), $(a_n-b_n)=\int f_n\to D$ is extremality of the sequence, and $A-\liminf b\le If$ is eq. (7) minus eq. (8). Under these, $b_n=a_n-(a_n-b_n)$ converges to $A-D$, so $\liminf b=A-D$ and $\limsup(a_n-b_n)=D$, giving both claimed equalities and $D\le\int f$. The middle equality -- the mixed $\lim$/$\liminf$/$\limsup$ step -- is therefore correct, and the asymmetry (a $\liminf$ on the left becoming a $\limsup$ after negation) is handled the right way round. Compiled clean, no `sorry`, standard axioms only.

f is not the constantly zero function. Therefore, f(0) ≠ 0. If 0 < f(0) < 1, then the function h := f / f(0) is in 𝒢_G(Ω) and has

THEOREM 9. Let G be a LCA group and Ω a closed neighbourhood of 0 with finite Haar measure. There exists an extremal function for D_G(Ω). Moreover, the extremal function can be approximated uniformly on the compact subsets of G by a D_G(Ω)-extremal sequence.

PROOF. On account of Theorem 3, let H be an open σ-compact subgroup of G containing Ω such that D_G(Ω) = D_H(Ω). By Theorem 8, there exists an extremal function f ∈ 𝒢_H(Ω) such that

∫_H f(g) dλ_H(g) = D_H(Ω).

Let f̃ be the trivial extension of f. By Lemma 1, f̃ ∈ 𝒢_G(Ω). We claim that f̃ is an extremal function for D_G(Ω). Indeed,

∫_G f̃(g) dλ_G(g) = ∫_H f(g) dλ_H(g) = D_H(Ω) = D_G(Ω).

As in Theorem 8, (f_n)_{n∈ℕ} converges to f uniformly on the compact subsets of H, and hence (f̃_n)_{n∈ℕ} converges to f̃ uniformly on the compact subsets of G. □
results.route_rationale: Main theorem and its proof; a short assembly of Theorem 3, Theorem 8 and Lemma 1.

fallback_result.reasoning: Theorem 9 and proof. The assembly is valid. Theorem 3 supplies an open $\sigma$-compact $H\supset\Omega$ with $\mathcal{D}_G(\Omega)=\mathcal{D}_H(\Omega)$; Theorem 8 applies to $H$ because $\Omega=\Omega\cap H$ is closed in $H$, is a neighbourhood of $0$ in $H$ ($H$ is open in $G$), and has finite $\lambda_H$-measure. Lemma 1 lifts the extremal $f\in\mathcal{G}_H(\Omega)$ to $\tilde f\in\mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)$ with $\int_G\tilde f\,d\lambda_G=\int_H f\,d\lambda_H=\mathcal{D}_H(\Omega)=\mathcal{D}_G(\Omega)$, so $\tilde f$ is extremal. The final approximation claim is also correct: for $K\subset G$ compact, $K\cap H$ is compact ($H$ is closed, being an open subgroup) and both $\tilde f_n$ and $\tilde f$ vanish on $K\setminus H$, so $\sup_K|\tilde f_n-\tilde f|=\sup_{K\cap H}|f_n-f|\to 0$. No error.

summary:
Mathematical verification of *On the Existence of an Extremal Function for the Delsarte Extremal Problem* (Analysis Mathematica 51, 2025). 25 self-contained mathematical objects were extracted: 19 went to informal review (`verify-math`) and 6 to formal Lean 4 verification (`verify-math-lean`), all six pinned to the shared reused project `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper` (Mathlib v4.33.1).

**What Lean settled.** All 6 Lean snippets returned `PASSED` -- compiled clean, no `sorry`, no `sorryAx`, and axioms exactly `[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]` in every case. These were chosen as the load-bearing steps where an error would actually hide:
- `PROPOSITION::0` -- $|f(g)|\le f(0)$ proved from the paper's own finite-double-sum definition of positive definiteness over an arbitrary abelian group, with no added hypotheses, plus the corollary that $f(0)=0$ forces $f\equiv 0$.
- `PROOF_STEP::0` -- equations (2), (3), (4): the integral splits over $H$ and $G\setminus H$, the tail integral is $\le 0$, hence $\int_H f_n\ge\int_G f_n$. The direction of (4) is confirmed.
- `PROOF_STEP::2` -- the convex-combination estimate $|\int h_n-D|\le\sum_k c_k^n|\int f_k-D|<\varepsilon$, including the *strictness*, which rests on $\sum_k c_k^n=1$ forcing some $c_{k_0}^n>0$.
- `PROOF_STEP::3` -- the whole chain (5)-(6): $\int f_+\le\lambda_G(\Omega)$, Fatou, the step $\int(f_n)_-\le\int(f_n)_+$ from $0\le\int f_n$, and $\int|f|=\int f_++\int f_-<\infty$.
- `PROOF_STEP::4` -- the mixed $\lim$/$\liminf$/$\limsup$ identity $\lim\int(f_n)_+-\liminf\int(f_n)_-=\limsup\int f_n$, the most error-prone step in the proof; it is correct, and the $\liminf\to\limsup$ flip under negation is done the right way round.
- `PROOF_STEP::5` -- the normalisation $f(0)=1$.

**What Lean could not settle, and was reviewed informally instead.** The paper lives in locally compact abelian group theory -- Haar measure, Bochner's theorem, integrally positive definite functions, weak $L^2$ compactness, Mazur's lemma -- essentially none of which exists in Mathlib at the required level. So Theorem 3's construction of $H$, Lemmas 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, Theorem 6 and the two main theorems (8 and 9) rest on informal review only. Those reviews were substantive rather than cursory: Lemma 4's constant was cross-checked numerically on $f=\cos$ and $f=e^{-|x|}$ over $G=\mathbb{R}$ and against the equivalent form $2f(0)[f(0)-\operatorname{Re}(f*\chi)(0)]$; Lemma 5's substitution $y=x+g$ was verified; Theorem 3's coset-counting step was reconstructed ($I_n=\{i:\lambda_G(A_i)>1/n\}$ is finite, so uncountably many disjoint positive-measure subsets of a finite-measure set is genuinely contradictory); and `PROPOSITION::1`'s unproved integrability assertion was independently confirmed via a Fejer-type weight argument.

**Disagreements.** None. No Lean result conflicts with an informal one, and no fallback passes were needed (no `FAILED`, no `NOT_ATTEMPTED`).

**Minor, non-erratum observations** (all below the 0.7 reporting threshold, recorded here rather than as findings): (i) Theorem 3's degenerate case sets both sides of (1) to $0$, i.e. tacitly adopts $\sup\emptyset=0$, a convention the paper never states; (ii) the proof of Theorem 8 says $\mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)$ sits in a 'closed, bounded, and hence a weakly sequentially compact' subset of $L^2(G)$ -- norm-closed plus bounded does not by itself give weak sequential compactness, but only boundedness is actually used to extract the weakly convergent subsequence, so the conclusion stands; (iii) the normalisation case split considers only $f(0)=0$ and $0<f(0)<1$, which is complete only because $f(0)\le 1$ was established earlier -- true, but not spelled out at that point; (iv) $\mathcal{D}_G(\Omega)>0$ is used without comment (it follows from $\Omega$ being a neighbourhood of $0$); (v) two typographical slips, $d\lambda_G(\Omega)$ for $d\lambda_G(g)$, in the displays near the end of Theorem 8's proof; (vi) the Uniform Boundedness Principle is invoked redundantly in Lemma 5. Outer regularity is also used to produce an open *identity neighbourhood* containing $\Omega$, which needs the one-line fix of replacing $U$ by $U\cup V$.

**Verdict.** NO_ERRORS. Every machine-checkable step of the two main proofs passed formal verification, and the remaining LCA-theoretic scaffolding survived careful informal review. Confidence is held at 0.82 rather than higher because Theorems 8 and 9 themselves, and Lemmas 4-7, carry only informal evidence.
